claims.claim: The DUNGEON staff say the key to designing a compelling fantasy city is presenting a strong sense of place.
claims.source: The DUNGEON Staff, DUNGEON Submission Guidelines, Appendix 1: Cities of Adventure
claims.quote: compelling fantasy city is presenting a strong “sense of place.”
claims.page: Appendix 1: Cities of Adventure, Thirty Questions About Your City

claims.claim: The DUNGEON staff set a writer thirty questions about a city before writing it, opening with who rules the city and how the ruler maintains power.
claims.source: The DUNGEON Staff, DUNGEON Submission Guidelines, Appendix 1: Cities of Adventure

claims.claim: Among the thirty questions the DUNGEON staff require a city writer to answer is what the city smells like.
claims.source: The DUNGEON Staff, DUNGEON Submission Guidelines, Appendix 1, question 24
claims.quote: What does the city smell like?

claims.claim: The last of the DUNGEON staff's thirty city questions, and the only one set in capitals, asks why adventurers come to the city.
claims.source: The DUNGEON Staff, DUNGEON Submission Guidelines, Appendix 1, question 30
claims.quote: WHY DO ADVENTURERS COME TO YOUR CITY?

claims.claim: A DUNGEON "Cities of Adventure" article runs from 8,000 to 10,000 words.
claims.source: The DUNGEON Staff, DUNGEON Submission Guidelines, Features
claims.quote: Cities of Adventure articles range in length from

claims.claim: A DUNGEON city article must carry a brief appendix with up to five complete stat blocks for personages important to the city.
claims.source: The DUNGEON Staff, DUNGEON Submission Guidelines, Features
claims.quote: stat blocks for personages important to the city

claims.claim: The DUNGEON staff hold that a background that cannot be presented in 500 words is probably too complex and should be simplified.
claims.source: The DUNGEON Staff, DUNGEON Submission Guidelines, Adventure Background
claims.quote: present an adventure background in 500 words, it’s probably

claims.claim: The DUNGEON guidelines list rumours, researchable background and town statistics among the sections a writer may place before an adventure's encounters.
claims.source: The DUNGEON Staff, DUNGEON Submission Guidelines, The Adventure's Encounters
claims.quote: background information the players can uncover in research

claims.claim: The Dragon editorial staff state that they will not publish an article written in the first person.
claims.source: Dragon Writers Guidelines (Dragon editorial staff), Format and Style
claims.quote: we will not publish an article written in the first person

claims.claim: The Dragon guidelines cap an article's opening narrative vignette or example dialogue at 200 words.
claims.source: Dragon Writers Guidelines (Dragon editorial staff), Format and Style

claims.claim: The Dragon guidelines require article manuscripts to use the current style of D&D game products, italicising magic item and spell names and capitalising feat names.
claims.source: Dragon Writers Guidelines (Dragon editorial staff), Format and Style
claims.quote: should use the current style of D&D game

claims.claim: Chris Sims, a D&D editor at Wizards of the Coast, says that as an editor he cuts weasel words without mercy.
claims.source: Chris S. Sims, Writing: Generalizations and Absolutes, 2020
claims.quote: As an editor, I cut weasel words without mercy.

claims.claim: Sims names generally and typically among the weasel words he objects to.
claims.source: Chris S. Sims, Writing: Generalizations and Absolutes, 2020
claims.quote: words such as generally, typically, and similar weasels

claims.claim: Sims says he has yet to see a superlative that was necessary for the fiction or mechanic in which it appeared.
